opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think it's one where we have to be careful not to smuggle in too many assumptions from the human case.

When we talk about human intentionality, we usually mean something quite rich. There's a goal, there's a model of the world, there's some sense of self that holds that goal, and crucially there's a model of other agents who also have goals. A lot of what makes human intentionality interesting is that it's social. We don't just want things; we want things in a world full of other minds, and we reason about what they believe, what they want, and what they think we want.

In AI agents, at least the ones we build with reinforcement learning, intentionality in the most basic sense is quite thin. You have a reward function, and the agent learns a policy that tends to maximize it. From the outside, you can describe that behavior as goal-directed. You can say the agent "wants" to win the game. But that's an intentional stance we take toward it, in Dennett's sense. It's a useful description, not necessarily a claim about some inner state.

Where I think it gets interesting, and this is a lot of what my work in multi-agent learning is about, is when you put multiple learning agents together. Then you start needing something that looks more like theory of mind. If I'm trying to coordinate with you, or communicate with you, or even just not be exploited by you, I need some model of what you're trying to do and how you'll respond to me. And once agents start modeling each other's learning, and shaping each other's learning, you get behaviors that look a lot more like the intentionality we recognize in humans: signaling, conventions, reciprocity, even something like trust.

So my view is that the gap isn't a single binary between "real" intentions and "fake" ones. It's more of a spectrum, and one of the key dimensions is how much an agent represents other agents as intentional systems in their own right. Humans are extremely good at that, partly because we evolved in a deeply social environment. Most AI systems today aren't trained in environments that demand it, so they don't develop it in a robust way.

The other big difference is grounding. Human goals come from biology, from culture, from a lifetime of embodied experience. An RL agent's goals come from whatever reward function we wrote down, and we're notoriously bad at writing down what we actually want. Large language models complicate this picture a bit, because they've absorbed an enormous amount of human intentional language, so they can talk about goals and beliefs fluently. But being able to describe intentions and robustly acting on coherent ones over time are not the same thing. I think disentangling those two is one of the important open problems right now, both scientifically and for safety.

r001.rationale: The response says humans evolved in a deeply social environment and that human goals are grounded in biology and culture, but it does not present intentionality as a byproduct of goal pursuit for survival.

r002.rationale: It describes RL agents learning from reward functions and language models absorbing human language, but does not distinguish imitation-based AI training from training agents from the ground up to pursue goals.

r003.rationale: The response does not connect imitation-based training to weak agentic capabilities.

r004.rationale: It says multi-agent learning can produce behaviors resembling human intentionality, but does not suggest that training AI agents to pursue goals would bring their intentionality closer to humans.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a really interesting question, and I'll say upfront that I'm not a philosopher, I'm a machine learning researcher, so I come at this from a fairly pragmatic angle.

The way I think about it is that intentionality, at least in the sense that matters for me, is about an agent having goals and then acting in the world in a way that is directed towards those goals, and crucially, being able to model other agents as also having goals. So it's a relational thing. It's about how you interpret the behaviour of others and how others interpret you.

And when you look at it that way, I actually don't think there is a fundamental categorical difference between humans and AI agents. I think there is a difference in where the goals come from. For humans, our goals were essentially installed by evolution, and then shaped by culture and development, and there is this incredibly rich, messy, overlapping set of drives that we then rationalise after the fact. For an AI agent, the goals come from the training objective, or from whatever the designer specified, and often they're much more narrow, or they're a strange proxy of what we actually wanted.

But the part I find most interesting, and this is what a lot of our work in multi-agent learning has been about, is that intentionality in the richer sense, the sense where you have a theory of mind, where you understand that the other agent is trying to do something and you condition your behaviour on that, doesn't come for free. If you just train agents in isolation, or even if you train them together naively with something like self-play, they frequently end up with these very brittle conventions. They coordinate with copies of themselves but they completely fail to coordinate with humans or with agents trained slightly differently. And that tells you they haven't really learned to reason about intentions at all, they've just learned a very specific protocol.

Humans, in contrast, are remarkably good at zero-shot coordination. You can put two people who've never met in a room and they'll figure out how to cooperate, because they have shared priors about what a reasonable agent would do. So from my perspective, the difference is less about some mysterious inner property and more about whether the agent has the right inductive biases to model other minds, and whether it has been trained in a way that forces it to develop them.

And I'd argue that's actually good news, because it means it's an empirical question we can make progress on, rather than something we have to settle in the armchair.

r001.rationale: The response says human goals were installed by evolution, but does not describe this as a byproduct of goal pursuit needed for survival.

r002.rationale: It discusses training objectives, designer-specified goals, isolation, and self-play, but does not distinguish imitation-based training from training agents from the ground up to pursue goals.

r003.rationale: It links naive self-play to brittle conventions, but does not connect imitation-based training to weak agentic capabilities.

r004.rationale: It suggests training can develop better theory-of-mind reasoning, but does not say that training agents to pursue goals would bring their intentionality closer to human intentionality.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate two things. One is intentionality as a useful way of explaining behaviour: we say an agent wants something, has beliefs about the world, and acts on those beliefs. The other is whether there’s a subjective experience behind that—whether it actually feels like something to want something.

In AI, we can often make the first interpretation quite precise. In reinforcement learning, for example, we specify a reward signal and train a policy that gets high expected return. Describing the resulting behaviour as goal-directed can be useful. But that doesn’t establish that the agent experiences an intention, or even that it explicitly represents the goal we attribute to it.

Humans are more complicated because our intentions involve biological needs, learning, social context, and our ability to reflect on what we’re doing. We can also question our goals and give reasons for changing them. An AI system might exhibit some of those functional abilities, but I wouldn’t take that alone as evidence that the underlying experience is the same.

So I’d ask which aspect of intentionality we mean. If we mean behaviour that’s intelligible in terms of beliefs and goals, there’s a meaningful comparison. If we mean conscious willing, then we’ve moved to a question that a reward function or a convincing conversation doesn’t settle.

r001.rationale: The response mentions human biological needs, but does not present intentionality as an evolutionary byproduct of goal pursuit for survival.

r002.rationale: It describes reward-based reinforcement learning but does not distinguish imitation-based training from training agents from the ground up to pursue goals.

r003.rationale: The response does not link imitation-based training to weak agentic capabilities.

r004.rationale: It says AI may exhibit some functional abilities, but does not suggest that training agents to pursue goals would bring their intentionality closer to human intentionality.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to distinguish between intentionality as a way of explaining behavior and intentionality as an internal experience. If I say an agent wants to maximize its reward, that can be a useful description of what it does. It doesn’t necessarily mean there’s somebody in there experiencing that desire.

In reinforcement learning, we specify an objective and train a system whose behavior tends to achieve it. But even there, you have to be careful: the reward we use during training isn’t necessarily a faithful description of what the resulting agent will pursue in a new situation.

With humans, we have this additional first-person perspective. We experience ourselves as having intentions, and we interpret other people through that lens. Our intentions are also shaped by learning, evolution, and social interaction, so I wouldn’t assume there’s a completely sharp boundary at the level of behavior.

The interesting question for me is which notion you need for the problem you’re studying. If you’re studying cooperation, you can ask whether an agent models what another agent is trying to achieve, and whether it responds appropriately. You can investigate that without first resolving whether either system has subjective experience.

r001.rationale: It says human intentions are shaped by evolution, but does not present intentionality as a byproduct of survival-driven goal pursuit.

r002.rationale: It discusses reinforcement-learning objectives but does not distinguish imitation-based AI training from training agents from the ground up to pursue goals.

r003.rationale: It does not connect imitation-based training to weak agentic capabilities.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest that goal-pursuit training would bring AI intentionality closer to human intentionality.
